title: Prevalence and patterns of convergent ecomorphological evolution in rodents
content:
Abstract
Convergent evolution occurs when independent adaptations to similar conditions lead to species that are more similar than expected given their phylogenetic relatedness. Despite its putative ubiquity in nature, studies of convergence often focus on few examples, and are limited by available data and tools. Leveraging data from specimens in Natural History Collections, we can test whether species with similar forms and lifestyles have more resemblance than can be explained by chance and phylogeny. Rodents are rarely investigated for convergence despite exemplifying ecological specialization with and without radical morphological changes. We investigated morphological convergence for 318 species using measurements from museum specimens. To quantify convergence, we applied Ornstein–Uhlenbeck models to identify shifts towards similar evolutionary regimes on the phylogeny and determined the strength of convergence using the Wheatsheaf and ct1 measures. We compared our results with existing ecomorph classifications, which should capture underlying evolutionary processes including convergence. We found numerous lineages that evolved similarities in some traits while maintaining distinct morphologies, and little convergence within ecomorphs.
